Author

Scheryll Ouma

Published

October 23, 2026

GitHub repo: https://github.com/scheryllouma/ec522_ps3_ouma

library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)

# Explicit column types; "." is FRED's missing-value marker
retail_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/retail_sales_raw.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    RSAFS = col_double(),
    RSAFSNA = col_double()
  )
)

retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA),
               names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")

retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)

can_gas <- canadian_gas |> select(Month, Volume)

1. Time and Tsibbles

The two datasets

retail_ts is U.S. Census Bureau advance retail and food services sales, downloaded manually from FRED. It is monthly, in millions of dollars, and contains two series stacked in long format: RSAFS (seasonally adjusted) and RSAFSNA (not seasonally adjusted). Its index is Month (a yearmonth) and its key is series_id.

can_gas is Canadian natural gas production (the canadian_gas dataset from the fpp3 package). It is monthly, with Volume in billions of cubic metres. Its index is Month and it has no key, because it holds only one series.

2.1–2.2 Reading the FRED file and checking dates

# 2.2a: let readr guess the column types
retail_guess <- read_csv("data/retail_sales_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(retail_guess)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  observation_date  RSAFS RSAFSNA
  <date>            <dbl>   <dbl>
1 1992-01-01       159177  142051
2 1992-02-01       159189  142498
3 1992-03-01       158647  154439
4 1992-04-01       159921  158430
5 1992-05-01       160471  164788
6 1992-06-01       161205  163417
guess_class <- class(retail_guess$observation_date)[1]

2.2a. In the guessed read-in, observation_date has class Date. FRED writes dates in ISO-8601 (YYYY-MM-DD), which read_csv() normally recognises. Even so, I re-read the file with explicit col_types (below). I learned why this matters: at one point my copy of the file had been opened and re-saved in Excel, which rewrote the dates as M/D/YYYY. My %Y-%m-%d format then turned every date into NA, and problems() showed the mismatch. Replacing the file with the untouched FRED download fixed it. The na = "." argument also matters, because FRED marks missing values with a period, and without it a single . would turn a numeric column into text.

# 2.2b: explicit column types (this is the version used throughout)
glimpse(retail_raw)
Rows: 417
Columns: 3
$ observation_date <date> 1992-01-01, 1992-02-01, 1992-03-01, 1992-04-01, 1992…
$ RSAFS            <dbl> 159177, 159189, 158647, 159921, 160471, 161205, 16285…
$ RSAFSNA          <dbl> 142051, 142498, 154439, 158430, 164788, 163417, 16457…

2.3 Wide vs. long

head(retail_raw)       # wide
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  observation_date  RSAFS RSAFSNA
  <date>            <dbl>   <dbl>
1 1992-01-01       159177  142051
2 1992-02-01       159189  142498
3 1992-03-01       158647  154439
4 1992-04-01       159921  158430
5 1992-05-01       160471  164788
6 1992-06-01       161205  163417
head(retail_raw_long)  # long
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  observation_date series_id  sales
  <date>           <chr>      <dbl>
1 1992-01-01       RSAFS     159177
2 1992-01-01       RSAFSNA   142051
3 1992-02-01       RSAFS     159189
4 1992-02-01       RSAFSNA   142498
5 1992-03-01       RSAFS     158647
6 1992-03-01       RSAFSNA   154439

2.3. In the wide tibble (retail_raw) there is one row per month and one column per series, so the series identity lives in the column names (RSAFS, RSAFSNA) and the table has 417 rows. In the long tibble (retail_raw_long) there is one row per month-series pair: the old column names become values of series_id and all numbers share one sales column, giving 834 rows (2 × 417). Long format is what ggplot2, autoplot() and grouped operations expect, since “which series is this?” becomes a usable variable.

2.5. Unlike retail_ts, canadian_gas has no # Key: line and key_vars() returns an empty result, because it holds a single series. Its index is Month (index_var() returns "Month") and the production variable is Volume. It runs from 1960 Jan to 2005 Feb (542 months), and it has no gaps.

2.6 Working with dates in a tsibble

# 2.6a: January 1990 onward
can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan"))
head(can_gas_recent)
# A tsibble: 6 x 2 [1M]
     Month Volume
     <mth>  <dbl>
1 1990 Jan   12.5
2 1990 Feb   11.2
3 1990 Mar   11.6
4 1990 Apr   11.1
5 1990 May   11.0
6 1990 Jun   10.1
# 2.6b: year, month label, quarter
can_gas_recent <- can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(year    = year(Month),
         month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),
         quarter = quarter(Month))

avg_by_month <- can_gas_recent |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume))

avg_by_month |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
month avg_volume
Jan 16.99
Feb 15.28
Mar 16.34
Apr 15.74
May 15.75
Jun 14.94
Jul 15.60
Aug 15.62
Sep 15.13
Oct 16.16
Nov 16.18
Dec 17.15

2.6b. Since 1990, the calendar month with the highest average production is Dec (17.15) and the lowest is Jun (14.94). Production is high in the winter months and lowest in summer, a pattern I come back to in Part 4.

# 2.6c: date arithmetic on a yearmonth index
can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(next_month = Month + 1,
         same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
  head()
# A tsibble: 6 x 7 [1M]
     Month Volume  year month quarter next_month same_month_last_year
     <mth>  <dbl> <dbl> <ord>   <int>      <mth>                <mth>
1 1990 Jan   12.5  1990 Jan         1   1990 Feb             1989 Jan
2 1990 Feb   11.2  1990 Feb         1   1990 Mar             1989 Feb
3 1990 Mar   11.6  1990 Mar         1   1990 Apr             1989 Mar
4 1990 Apr   11.1  1990 Apr         2   1990 May             1989 Apr
5 1990 May   11.0  1990 May         2   1990 Jun             1989 May
6 1990 Jun   10.1  1990 Jun         2   1990 Jul             1989 Jun

2.6c. Because Month is a yearmonth, + 1 moves forward one month and - 12 moves back exactly one year (the same month last year). For an ordinary calendar Date such as observation_date in retail_raw, adding 1 moves forward one day, so a yearmonth index is what makes month-based arithmetic safe.

# 2.6d: monthly -> quarterly (drop incomplete 2005 Q1)
can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))

head(can_gas_q)
# A tsibble: 6 x 2 [1Q]
  Quarter Volume
    <qtr>  <dbl>
1 1960 Q1   4.14
2 1960 Q2   3.30
3 1960 Q3   2.97
4 1960 Q4   4.26
5 1961 Q1   5.01
6 1961 Q2   4.17
can_gas_q |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production (Quarterly)", x = NULL,
       y = "Volume (billions of cubic metres)") +
  theme_minimal()

2.6d. The header now reads [1Q]. We sum() the monthly values because gas production is a flow: a quarter’s production is the total produced across its three months, whereas a mean() would give the average monthly rate and understate the quarter’s output by a factor of three. The quarterly series is still clearly seasonal: the same repeating within-year pattern (higher in winter quarters, lower in the third quarter) shows up around a rising trend. Aggregating to quarters shrinks the pattern to four points per year but does not remove it.

2.7 Plotting with autoplot()

# 2.7a
retail_ts |> autoplot(sales)
# 2.7b
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
       subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
       x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

2.7b. The NSA series (RSAFSNA) swings sharply around the SA series (RSAFS) every year, with a spike around the holiday season (December) and a drop in the early months of the year, repeating at the same time each year. The SA series does not have this pattern and is much smoother. In the long run the two lines follow the same path: the same upward trend, and the same large shocks (the 2008–09 recession and the sharp April 2020 pandemic drop appear in both). So seasonal adjustment removes the predictable within-year cycle but leaves the trend and the genuine economic shocks in place.

# 2.7c
can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production", x = NULL,
       y = "Volume (billions of cubic metres)") +
  theme_minimal()
# 2.7d: comma-formatted y axis on the retail plot
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales (comma-formatted axis)",
       subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
       x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

2.7d. I added scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) to the retail plot, replacing scientific notation such as 6e+05 with readable numbers like 600,000, so the dollar amounts can be read at a glance.

2. Transformations

3.1 Log transformation

# level plot, for reference (from 2.7c)
can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production (level)", x = NULL, y = "Volume") +
  theme_minimal()
# 3.1b: add log_volume and plot it
can_gas <- can_gas |> mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production (log scale)", x = NULL,
       y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()

3.1a. In the level plot the seasonal swings grow as the series grows through the early part of the sample: in the 1960s, when production is low, the swings are small in absolute terms, and they become much larger through the 1970s and 1980s as the level rises. But this is not true over the whole sample. After roughly 1990, production keeps growing, yet the seasonal swings get smaller, not larger, so the size of the swings changes in a way that is not simply proportional to the level.

3.1b. After taking logs, the steep early growth is compressed and the trend looks smoother and closer to a straight line for the first couple of decades, and the seasonal swings from the 1960s through the 1980s look comparable in size rather than ballooning with the level. However, the log plot also shows that the trend is not a single straight line (very steep growth in the 1960s, a plateau from the mid-1970s to the mid-1980s, renewed growth in the 1990s, flattening in the 2000s) and that the seasonal swings shrink noticeably after about 1990, which logs do not fix. My view is that logs are a good idea for can_gas, but not a complete fix. They help for the first half of the sample, where the swings grew with the level, and they give coefficients a percentage interpretation (used for the trend coefficient in 4.4a). But the changing seasonal amplitude and the bending trend remain after logging.

# 3.1c: NSA retail, level vs log
retail_nsa <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales))

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales (level)", x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()
retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales (log)", x = NULL, y = "log(sales)") +
  theme_minimal()

3.1c. In levels, the NSA retail seasonal swings clearly widen as sales rise, and the trend curves upward. After logging, the trend is close to a straight line and the seasonal swings are roughly the same size throughout the sample. The case for logging is therefore stronger here than for can_gas: retail sales shows the clean pattern of swings proportional to the level that logs remove, while can_gas had changing swing sizes and a bending trend that logs left behind.

3.2 Growth rates

# 3.2a: two ways of computing month-over-month growth
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct  = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume)
  )

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas: Month-over-Month Growth (direct)",
       x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(title = "Gap: Direct vs. Log-Difference Growth",
       x = NULL, y = "Absolute gap (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()

3.2a. Direct month-over-month growth is large and seasonal, with swings of roughly ±20% in the early decades that narrow in later years (to roughly ±10%). The gap between the direct and log-difference growth rates has a median of only 0.14 percentage points, but it spikes to a maximum of 3.26 points in months with very large changes, and it shrinks in the later years when growth rates are smaller. So the log-difference is a very good approximation for typical months and small growth rates, and a noticeably worse one in the rare months with changes of 20% or more.

3.3 SA vs. NSA growth rates

retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
       x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
retail_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(series_id) |>
  summarize(sd_growth = sd(growth_mom, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
series_id sd_growth
RSAFS 1.70
RSAFSNA 9.57

3.3. The NSA series is far noisier: its month-over-month growth swings between roughly −30% and +20% every year, with a standard deviation of 9.6%, compared with only 1.7% for the SA series, which stays close to zero apart from the 2020 pandemic shock. The reason is the one seen in 2.7b: the NSA series contains the predictable seasonal cycle (a big jump into December, a big fall in January), which shows up as large recurring spikes in month-to-month growth, whereas the SA series has had that cycle removed and mostly reflects genuine changes in the economy.

3. Seasonality

4.1 Season plots

# 4.1a: NSA retail
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()
# 4.1b: SA retail
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()
# 4.1c: Canadian gas (logged); no key, so no filter needed
can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in Canadian Gas Production (log)",
       y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()

4.1a–b. In the NSA season plot, every year’s line traces the same recognisable shape (a dip in the early months, a build through the year and a spike in December), so the lines run in parallel, stacked by the level of that year. In the SA season plot the lines are close to flat and show no consistent within-year shape; the only visible departure is the sharp dip of the 2020 line in the spring. This is what “seasonally adjusted” means: the SA series is the NSA series with the repeating seasonal pattern estimated and removed.

4.1c. Logged gas production is high in winter (December through February) and lowest in the summer months (roughly June through September), a U-shaped pattern across the year, with a visible dip in February (a shorter month) in many years. This matches intuition: natural gas is used heavily for heating, so Canadian demand and production are highest in the cold months. The season plot also shows that the seasonal swing is much smaller in recent years (the top lines are flatter) than in earlier decades, consistent with 3.1.

4.2 Subseries plot

can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)")
lv_month <- can_gas |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(m = month(Month, label = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(m) |>
  summarize(avg_log_volume = mean(log_volume))

4.2. Each panel shows one calendar month across all years, with the blue line at that month’s average. The averages are highest in Dec and lowest in Jun, confirming the winter-high, summer-low pattern. All twelve panels show the same long-run shape (steep growth, then a plateau), which tells us that the trend, not the seasonal pattern, drives most of the variation over time, and that every month shares that trend.

4.3 X-13ARIMA-SEATS

# 4.3a
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
x13_month <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(m = month(Month, label = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(m) |>
  summarize(sf = mean(seasonal))

dec <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(month(Month) == 12)

4.3a. The seasonal factor is highest in Dec, where on average sales are about 14.8% above trend. The December factor was 1.21 in 1992 (about 21% above trend) and 1.1 in 2025 (about 10%). So the size of the seasonal swings changes over time: it shrinks, as the seasonal panel of the decomposition shows, with taller peaks and deeper troughs in the early years than in recent ones. The irregular component is close to 1 except for the 2020 pandemic shock.

# 4.3b
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
       x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
worst <- sa_compare |> slice_max(abs(pct_diff), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

4.3b. My default-settings X-13 adjustment tracks the Census Bureau’s official series closely: the mean absolute difference is 0.21%, and 93% of months differ by less than half a percent, with the differences centred on zero. The largest gaps occur around the 2020–2021 pandemic period (the single largest is 1.78% in 2022 Jan), when unusual swings make the choice of outlier treatment matter most. This is expected: the Census Bureau tailors the settings for each series (holiday and trading-day effects, outliers) and adjusts the individual retail categories separately before adding them up, whereas I ran the program once on the total with defaults.

coefs <- can_gas_fit |> tidy()
trend_coef <- coefs$estimate[coefs$term == "trend()"]
seas <- coefs |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "season")) |>
  mutate(m = as.integer(str_extract(term, "\\d+")),
         month_name = month.name[m])
top_seas <- seas |> slice_max(abs(statistic), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

4.4a. The trend() coefficient is 0.004, so the estimated average monthly growth rate of gas production is about 0.4% (the coefficient times 100, since the dependent variable is in logs). This is an average over the whole 1960–2005 sample and hides the fact that growth was very fast early on and much slower later. The seasonal dummy with the largest t-statistic in absolute value is June (coefficient -0.251, t = -4.8), meaning that month is on average lower than January relative to trend (January is the omitted base month). The summer dummies are negative, consistent with the winter-high seasonal pattern. Because the residuals are strongly autocorrelated (4.4c), these standard errors and t-statistics are likely too optimistic and should be read cautiously.

# 4.4b
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

4.4b. The fitted line captures the regular seasonal oscillation well: the fitted and actual series rise and fall together within each year, and the fit is good around the late 1960s and again during the late 1980s to early 1990s. It misses the trend, because a single straight line cannot follow a series that grew very fast in the 1960s, flattened from the mid-1970s to the mid-1980s, grew again, and then levelled off. The fitted line is far too high at the very start, too low through the 1970s and early 1980s, and too high by the end of the sample.

# 4.4c
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()
lb <- can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24)

lb |> knitr::kable(digits = 4)
.model lb_stat lb_pvalue
TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()) 7774.218 0

4.4c. The residuals do not look like white noise. The time plot shows long, slow swings (strongly negative in the early 1960s, a large hump peaking in the early 1970s, then drifting down again), the ACF starts near 1 and decays only very slowly, staying far outside the dashed bounds even at lag 24, and the histogram is lumpy rather than bell-shaped. The Ljung–Box test with 24 lags gives a statistic of 7774.2 and a p-value of 0, so at the 5% level we reject the null of white noise: there is substantial remaining autocorrelation, and therefore forecastable structure, that the model has not captured.

4. Forecast Evaluation

5.1 Expanding-window TS-CV

gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

acc_exp <- gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))

acc_exp |> select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
.model MAE RMSE
snaive 0.562 0.702
tslm 4.009 4.362 
# errors lined up by month (used here and in 5.2)
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

best_mae  <- acc_exp$.model[which.min(acc_exp$MAE)]
best_rmse <- acc_exp$.model[which.min(acc_exp$RMSE)]
mae_of  <- function(m) round(acc_exp$MAE[acc_exp$.model == m], 3)
rmse_of <- function(m) round(acc_exp$RMSE[acc_exp$.model == m], 3)

5.1a. The first evaluated forecast is for 1980 Jan (the first training sample of 240 months ends December 1979) and the last is for 2005 Feb; the final window’s forecast for March 2005 cannot be evaluated because that month is not in the data. There are 302 evaluated one-month-ahead forecasts. The results are in the table above: the seasonal naive model has MAE 0.562 and RMSE 0.702, and the trend + seasonal dummies model has MAE 4.009 and RMSE 4.362. By MAE the more accurate model is snaive and by RMSE it is snaive, so the two metrics agree. The seasonal random walk is anchored to what happened one year ago, so it automatically follows wherever the series currently is. The linear trend + dummies model forecasts from a straight line, and since its residuals are strongly persistent (4.4c), whenever the actual series is far from the line, its one-month-ahead forecast is far off too.

5.2 Diebold–Mariano test

dm <- forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
dm

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  errs$snaiveerrs$tslm
DM = -31.278, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 1, p-value <
2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

5.2a. The DM statistic (absolute loss, power = 1) is -31.28 with a p-value of 1.39^{-96}. At the 5% level we reject the null that the two models forecast equally accurately. In words: the forecast errors of the two models are significantly different, and the sign of the statistic indicates that the seasonal naive model has the smaller absolute errors.

5.3 Rolling window

gas_roll_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

acc_roll <- gas_roll_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))

bind_rows(
  acc_exp  |> mutate(window = "Expanding"),
  acc_roll |> mutate(window = "Rolling (240)")
) |>
  select(window, .model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
window .model MAE RMSE
Expanding snaive 0.562 0.702
Expanding tslm 4.009 4.362
Rolling (240) snaive 0.562 0.702
Rolling (240) tslm 2.095 2.425 
chg <- function(a, b, m, col) round(b[[col]][b$.model == m] - a[[col]][a$.model == m], 3)

5.3a. Switching to a rolling window changes the MAE of the trend + seasonal dummies model by -1.914 and its RMSE by -1.938, while the seasonal naive model’s MAE changes by only 0. So the trend + seasonal dummies model’s accuracy changed much more. The reason is in the fitted values of 4.4b: one straight-line trend fitted to the full history is a poor description of a series whose trend bends and changes slope, so it gives stale forecasts. A rolling 240-month window re-estimates the trend (and seasonal pattern) using only the most recent 20 years, so the line adapts to the local slope and level. The seasonal naive model only looks at the same month one year earlier, so the length of the training window makes no difference to its forecasts (the forecast origins are the same in both schemes).

5. Reflection

The residuals from the trend + seasonal dummies model still looked like they were missing a lot of structure. They were slowly moving and highly autocorrelated (an ACF near 1 decaying slowly, and a Ljung–Box test rejecting white noise), tracing out the bends in the trend that a straight line cannot capture. The seasonal amplitude also changes over time (it shrinks in later years), which fixed seasonal dummies cannot accommodate. This showed up in the forecast evaluation: the seasonal naive benchmark, which simply tracks last year’s value, was the more accurate model (snaive has the lower MAE), and the DM test confirmed that the difference is statistically significant. Re-estimating on a rolling window helped the trend model because it let the trend adapt, which again points to the problem being a trend that is not constant. I would expect a model that captures the missing structure, for example one with a stochastic or flexible trend and autocorrelated errors (such as ARIMA or ETS, or a regression with ARMA errors), to produce residuals that look like white noise, with an ACF inside the bounds and a Ljung–Box test that does not reject.
